meaning: Each tie names the phrase of the paper that a Lean declaration states, as read side by side for Proof Reader (wcook04/proof-reader 3858afbe00b2, papers/navier-stokes-paper). Titles, reading notes, topics and comparisons are AI-drafted or AI-assessed; no mathematician has reviewed them.

families.name: From a certificate to a profile
From cell data to the certificate

topics.name: The blow-up statements
topics.description: Smooth solutions, breakdown on space and on the torus, and the theorems that state them (Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1).

topics.name: The fractional extension
topics.description: The authors' separate extension with dissipation exponent between 1 and 5/4, outside the classical paper.

topics.name: Heat flow and mild solutions
topics.description: The heat semigroup, the bilinear Duhamel term, mild solutions, restarting and uniqueness (§3).

topics.name: Recurrent profiles
topics.description: Self-similar time-periodic profiles, their slices and orbits, and weak profiles read as physical fields (§2, §4.1, §7.11).

topics.name: Monodromy and the correction
topics.description: The period map, its compact-plus-small splitting, the spectral projection and the fixed point that corrects a profile to an exact solution (§4).

topics.name: Passing to the torus
topics.description: The solenoidal cutoff, periodization and the periodic right inverse that move the construction onto the torus (§5–6).

topics.name: From certificate to profile
topics.description: Certificate data, the free operator, convection, held solutions and the smoothing of the weak profile they produce (§7).

topics.name: The coercive multiplier estimate
topics.description: The multiplier, its five density coefficients and lower bound, and the a priori estimate it gives (Appendix B.1 and B.2).

topics.name: Encoded cell data
topics.description: The finitely represented inputs: coordinates and harmonics, the profile representation, splines and jets, physical cells, rows, weights and potentials.

topics.name: Reduction to the quarter plane
topics.description: Symmetry reduction of the density to the meridian quarter plane (B.3).

topics.name: Cells, traces and tails
topics.description: Integrability, the common vector of unknowns, resolved modes, the tail budget and the exterior estimate (B.4).

topics.name: Angular and ray-exterior tests
topics.description: The angular inequalities, the pointwise test and the integrated test on ray exteriors (B.5 and B.6).

topics.name: The matrix tree lower bound
topics.description: The tree conditions on the cell matrices and the passage from all cells to the global inequality (B.7 and B.8).

topics.name: Changing the profile
topics.description: Bounds for moving estimates from the reference field to the actual profile (B.9).

topics.name: The adjoint pairing and its error
topics.description: The quadratic adjoint pairing, the azimuthal dual norm and the linear adjoint error with potentials and pins (B.10 to B.12).

topics.name: The offset and the certificate
topics.description: Enclosing the constant, linear and quadratic offset, and the fifteen fields of CellSystemCondition that make the data a certificate (B.13 and B.14).

notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectBou: For a fixed adjoint index $j$ and parameters in $\mathcal K$, this condition collects the numerical assumptions for the linear adjoint estimate. It bounds each coordinate $|\alpha_i|$ by $\bar\varrho_i$, using nonzero $d_i$ and $|\varrho_*|\le|d_i|\bar\varrho_i$ outside $\mathcal J$. For the central potentials it requires nonnegative bounds on $\|G_j\|_{\mathcal H}$, $\|\nabla U_j\|_{\mathcal H}$ and $\|F_j\|_{\mathcal H}$, and a dual bound on the residual. Every separately fitted direction has corresponding potential and residual bounds. On the remaining directions, $\varpi_i>0$, the weighted velocity norm is at most $n_{\mathrm v}$, and common dual bounds $n_i$ for $(\nabla W_\alpha^i)^{\mathsf T}\psi_j$ satisfy $\sum_i\varpi_i n_i^2\le n_{\mathrm d}^2$. It also requires a dual bound $n_\theta$ for $\partial_\theta\psi_j$, the constraint replacement norm $n_\Phi$, the uniform matrix error $c_\Xi$ for every coefficient vector, and $\|(Y_{jl})_l\|\le n_Y$. Finally the potential and parameter sum plus $n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$ is at most $a_j$. The paper's (B.53) is the case with no fitted directions. All norms are on $(0,1)\times\mathbb R^3$; matrix $L^2$ norms use the sum of squares of entries. This is a collection of assumptions. Regularity, decomposition identities and positivity of the weight are supplied separately before deriving (7.33).

This field of the adjoint-defect assumptions requires, for every real coefficient vector x∈ℝⁿ, ∫₀¹∫_{ℝ³}|∑ᵢx_i(Ξ_i−∇Φ_i)|_F²≤c_Ξ²∑ᵢx_i². The matrix square is the sum of squared Euclidean norms of its columns, so the left side is the squared H norm in the paper. The integral is initially nonnegative and may be infinite; the finite right side bounds it. Nonnegativity of c_Ξ is required elsewhere in the same data condition. Consequently this squared inequality gives ‖∑ᵢx_i(Ξ_i−∇Φ_i)‖_H≤c_Ξ|x|. The hypothesis concerns all x, including combinations of distinct constraints; it is stronger than independent bounds for the individual tensors.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AdjointDefectEnt: Let $w_*>0$. For potential bounds $n=(n_G,n_U,n_F,n_R)$ put $D(n)=\sqrt{n_G^2+(w_*n_U+n_F+n_R)^2/w_*}$. If a finite set $I$ of parameter directions has its own fitted potential bounds $n^{(i)}$, this definition is $D(n^{(0)})+\sum_{i\in I}\bar\varrho_iD(n^{(i)})+w_*^{-1/2}\{[\sum_{i\notin I}\bar\varrho_i^2/\varpi_i]^{1/2}(n_{\mathrm v}+n_{\mathrm d})+[\sum_{i\notin I}|\varsigma_i|\bar\varrho_i]n_\theta\}$. The paper-specific identification sets $I=\varnothing$, leaving the first two terms of (B.53). The constraint replacement charge is added separately. The definition itself accepts arbitrary real inputs and uses the formal zero value for division by zero; its application requires $w_*>0$ and $\varpi_i>0$, and nonnegative norm bounds. It is a proposed numerical budget, with no assertion here that the fields satisfy it.

This definition forms $n_\Phi+n_Yc_\Xi/\sqrt{w_*}$. Here $n_\Phi$ bounds $\|\sum_lY_{jl}(\Phi_l-\widetilde\Phi_l)\|_{\mathcal H}$, $n_Y$ bounds the Euclidean norm of the row $(Y_{jl})_l$, and $c_\Xi$ controls the $L^2$ matrix error in replacing $\Xi_l$ by $\nabla\Phi_l$. The two contributions pair with $\Delta v$ and $\nabla v$ respectively. For a positive constant weight they give the last part of (B.53) after division by the energy norm. This declaration defines the number; the assertions that it bounds those pairings, and that the indicated numbers bound the norms, are separate statements. Division by zero is defined to be zero, but the intended use has $w_*=39/50>0$.

For the fixed adjoint $\psi_j$, compact generators $\widetilde\Phi_l$ and real coefficients $Y_{jl}$, this definition forms $K=
abla\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l-(
abla\widetilde\Phi_l)^{\mathsf T})$. A gradient is represented by the map that sends a coordinate vector to the corresponding directional derivative. Thus the divergence of this matrix map is $\Delta\psi_j-\sum_lY_{jl}(\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l-
abla\operatorname{div}\widetilde\Phi_l)$. For the divergence-free generators of the paper, $-\operatorname{div}K=-\Delta\psi_j+\sum_lY_{jl}\Delta\widetilde\Phi_l$, which supplies precisely those terms in (B.52). The definition alone does not assert regularity or divergence-freeness. The skew part of the generator gradient is retained explicitly in the general formal construction.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalBounded: Let $R$ be a measurable real vector field on $\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y^3$, and let $n\ge0$. The condition represents each of $R_1+iR_2$, $R_1-iR_2$ and $R_3$, almost everywhere in $y$ for every $\theta$, as a finite sum $\sum e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$. Each amplitude is measurable and satisfies $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$ for every angle and point. The integers $k',k$ are distinct as pairs within each component. It requires $\sum c\,(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2\le n^2$, with $c=1/2$ for each horizontal complex component and $c=1$ for the third. The denominator is positive for every integer $k$, including zero. The representation implies period one almost everywhere; exact pointwise periodicity is not a separate assumption. These are the harmonic terms called $R''$ in the paper's dual bound.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.I: For real vectors $v,R\in\mathbb R^3$, define $v^+=v_1+iv_2$, $v^-=v_1-iv_2$ and $v^0=v_3$, and use the same convention for $R$. The formal statement proves $v\cdot R=\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^+}R^+)+\tfrac12\operatorname{Re}(\overline{v^-}R^-)+v_3R_3$. This is an identity of real numbers, with no regularity or integrability hypotheses. It is the component decomposition used at the end of the proof of Lemma B.11. The two horizontal factors are $1/2$; the vertical factor is $1$. The formal component labels begin at zero and refer in order to $+$, $-$ and the vertical component.

For any real matrix $M:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$, let $M^+$, $M^-$ and $M^0$ be the matrices obtained by taking the two horizontal rows as a complex pair, its conjugate, and the vertical row. The formal statement proves $\tfrac12|M^+|^2+\tfrac12|M^-|^2+|M^0|^2=|M|^2$, where the norms are sums of squared entries, and the complex pair is represented by its two real coordinates. Taking $M=\nabla v$ gives the weighted gradient identity in the proof of Lemma B.11. The formal theorem is purely algebraic for every matrix; applying it almost everywhere and integrating gives the same identity for any weakly differentiable field with finite gradient energy. No symmetry, periodicity or solenoidality is assumed.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.g: For a measurable matrix field $G:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^{3\times3}$, the formal statement proves that the sum over all integer azimuthal modes of its gradient energy in the rotating cylindrical frame is at most $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|G|^2$. The mode energy is integrated with cylindrical measure $2\pi r\,dr\,dz$ on $r>0$, $z\in\mathbb R$; the matrix norm on the right is the sum of squares of all entries. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The statement applies to any measurable matrix field, without requiring that it be the derivative of a velocity. This is the spatial Fourier-energy estimate used to pass from single-mode inequalities to the total bound. Projection in the time variable is a separate operation.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.m: Let $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and its weak gradient $G$ be measurable, with $v\in L^6$ and $G\in L^2$. Put $U=v_1+iv_2$, and let $U_k(r,z)$ be its normalized angular Fourier coefficient. Given the smooth azimuthal estimate, approximation by smooth compactly supported fields in gradient norm and local $L^2$, and the bound of the total Fourier gradient energy by $\int|G|^2$, the formal statement proves $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|U_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dr\,dz\le\int|G|^2$. Thus it controls all angular projections together. The paper states (B.50) for a single complex field already having wave number $k$; representing that field by two real components yields its special case. The three analytic premises are supplied by separate proved declarations in the packet. No divergence or reflection assumption on $v$ occurs.

Let $u,B:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb C$ be measurable, and assume $B(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)=e^{ik\phi}B(r,0,z)$ for an integer $k$. Let $u_k(r,z)$ be the angular coefficient normalized by $1/(2\pi)$. The formal statement gives $|\int\overline{u}B|^2\le[2\pi\int_{r>0,z\in\mathbb R}r|u_k|^2/(r^2+z^2)]\,[\int|y|^2|B|^2]$. This uses Cauchy–Schwarz after angular projection; combining it with the azimuthal Hardy estimate produces the factor $(|k|+1/2)^{-1}$ in the paper. The displayed conclusion uses the opposite complex conjugation from the paper's pairing, which has the same absolute value. No integrability premise is present in this particular declaration, and nonnegative integrals can be infinite; the surrounding dual-bound hypotheses supply finiteness and the integrability theorem supplies the integrable signed-pairing interpretation.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.s: Let $u:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ be smooth with compact support, and let $U=u_1+iu_2$. For any integer $k$, form the angular coefficient $U_k(r,z)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-ik\phi}U(r\cos\phi,r\sin\phi,z)\,d\phi$. The formal statement bounds $(|k|+1/2)^2\,2\pi\int_{r>0}\int_{\mathbb R}r|U_k(r,z)|^2/(r^2+z^2)\,dz\,dr$ by the corresponding Fourier component of the full gradient energy, represented in the rotating cylindrical frame. It is a statement about an angular projection of a smooth real vector field. Taking $u=(\operatorname{Re}U,\operatorname{Im}U,0)$ when $U$ already has wave number $k$ gives the smooth scalar inequality in (B.50). Extending to an $L^6$ field with a weak $L^2$ gradient requires the separate approximation result. The denominator is nonzero on $r>0$.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.t: Take a finite family of measurable complex amplitudes $a_p(y)$ and distinct integer temporal frequencies $k'_p$. The formal statement proves $\int_0^1\int|y|^2|\sum_p e^{2\pi i k'_p\theta}a_p(y)|^2\,dy\,d\theta\le\sum_p\int|y|^2|a_p(y)|^2\,dy$. Both sides are nonnegative extended integrals. The frequencies need be distinct only on the selected finite index set. In the adjoint proof this is applied separately to groups having the same azimuthal order, for which distinct pairs imply distinct temporal frequencies. Its conclusion is a weighted $L^2$ estimate for finite harmonic sums; the paper's displayed Bessel inequality concerns arbitrary space-time projections in gradient norm.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.AzimuthalParts.w: Let a measurable vector field $v:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ have measurable weak gradient $G$, with $v\in L^6$ and $\int|G|^2<\infty$. There exists a sequence of smooth compactly supported real vector fields $u_n$ such that $\int|\nabla u_n-G|^2\to0$ and, for every real radius $R$, $\int_{B_R}|u_n-v|^2\to0$. The ball is centered at the origin; for negative $R$ it is empty. A specified azimuthal wave number is preserved by the subsequent angular projection, which is a separate step. The conclusion here is the approximation before that projection. Complex scalar functions are handled by their real and imaginary parts. No solenoidality condition is required.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.DualBounded: A real field $R$ on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ has this bound $n$ when it is the pointwise sum of two measurable fields $R_h+R_p$, with nonnegative bounds $n_h,n_p$ satisfying $n_h+n_p\le n$. The ordinary part obeys $2\||y|R_p\|_{L^2((0,1)\times\mathbb R^3)}\le n_p$. In each complex component $R_{h,1}\pm iR_{h,2}$ and $R_{h,3}$, the harmonic part is a finite sum $e^{2\pi i k'\theta}g(y)$ of measurable amplitudes with distinct integer pairs $(k',k)$ and $g(R_\phi y)=e^{ik\phi}g(y)$. The sum of $(|k|+1/2)^{-2}\int|y|^2|g|^2$, with weight $1/2$ on each horizontal component, is at most $n_h^2$. This is the paper's decomposition with its two terms listed in reverse order. Unlike the surrounding prose, the definition does not require exact periodicity of the ordinary part. The resulting estimate concerns the single normalized interval $(0,1)$.
notes.Breakdown.AdjointDefect.Internal.Potenti: Let $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ have a measurable weak gradient $\nabla v\in L^2$. Suppose a locally integrable matrix field $A$ has the stated distributional divergence $d$, and for some $a>3/2$ and constant $B$ one has $|A(y)|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ everywhere and $|y||d(y)|\le B(1+|y|)^{-a}$ almost everywhere. Then $v\cdot d$ is integrable and $\int v\cdot d=-\int\nabla v:A$. The decay implies the $L^2$ conditions on $A$ and $|y|d$ used in the weak pairing theorem. This is the form needed for the potential fluxes. It has a narrower decay-based hypothesis than the printed general (B.55), while giving the same integration-by-parts identity in this application.

Fix a time $	heta$, a real constant $w_*$ and a divergence-free $v\in L^6$ with weak gradient and Hessian, $
abla v,\Delta v\in L^2$. Assume L>0, κ>0 and an admissible C³ radial phase and origin function, together with the scalar pressure data of B.1: continuous piecewise polynomials, h≥2, the stated origin and axis factors, and conjugation and reflection. The theorem proves that the real scalar q(θ,y) is jointly continuous, has period 1 in θ, and on each closed spatial ball is Lipschitz in y with one constant valid for all real θ. It does not claim C¹ regularity of q across its polynomial interfaces. The derivative is therefore understood almost everywhere for integration by parts; separate results identify the resulting gradient as orthogonal to solenoidal tests.

The shape hypotheses are these. Let L>0 and κ∈ℕ with κ>0. Let f:ℝ→ℝ be C³ on (−δ,∞) for some δ>0, with |sf′(s)|, |s²f″(s)| and |s³f‴(s)| bounded for s≥0. Let g(σ) be a real polynomial up to 0<σ_g≤1 and a constant afterward, with g(0)=1; when σ_g<1 the values and the first two derivatives join at σ_g. No join beyond σ=1 is required.  The scalar amplitude condition is the following. The scalar q is the real part of a finite sum of E_{ι,l}σ^{h₀}(1−σ)^h(1−η²)^{h′}P(σ,η). This condition imposes natural-number exponents, h≥2, and continuous complex polynomial pieces on rectangular meshes. It requires h′≥1 when ι₁≠0 and h′=0 when ι₁=0. For h₀=0 the value of P at σ=0 is zero in nonzero azimuthal modes and is constant in η in zero modes. The set of modes is closed under conjugation and reflection; their exponents agree, their coefficients are conjugated for (−ι,−l), and P(σ,−η) is used for (ι^♭,l). The condition is on the coefficients, with phase and length conditions supplied separately. It neither fixes a pressure gauge nor solves a Poisson equation. Here σ=|y|/(|y|+L), η=y₃/|y| and E_{ι,l}=exp(i[2π(2ι₂−ι₁)θ+κι₁φ+lf(|y|²)]), with φ=arg(y₁+iy₂) and ι^♭=(−ι₁,ι₂−ι₁). The partitions have domains [0,1] and [−1,1]. At y=0 the quotients by |y| and the angle are assigned zero. Positivity of L and κ and the regularity of f are separate shape assumptions.

notes.Breakdown.CellReduction.Instantiation.sc: Let p:ℝ×ℝ³→ℝ be jointly continuous and, at every real θ, locally Lipschitz in y on every closed ball. The theorem proves measurability of the spatial gradient field and ∫_{ℝ×ℝ³}∇_yp·φ=0 for every smooth compactly supported divergence-free vector test field φ. The Lipschitz constants may depend on θ and on the ball in this statement. The formal statement asserts a bounded linear map $U:\ell^\infty(E)\to E$ with $PUc=Uc$, and a real $K'$, such that if $Px_0=Uc$, then the recurrence $x_{n+1}=\Theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ obeys $\|x_n\|\le K'(\|x_0\|+\|c\|_{\ell^\infty})$ for every natural $n$. The datum’s stable component is free; its projected component is selected from the entire future source sequence.

The statement requires no finite-rank assumption. It is an estimate for a normalized sequence, not for a global physical-time curve.

This declaration specifies the assertion; it supplies no proof by itself.
notes.Breakdown.EnergyBoundedOn: For a field $U:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $T\in\mathbb R$, the formal condition is that some finite constant bounds $\int_{\mathbb R^3}|U(t,x)|^2\,dx$ for every $t\in[0,T]$. The integral is the extended nonnegative integral of the squared Euclidean norm. In the formula, a real bound $A$ is replaced by $\max(A,0)$; the existential condition is therefore equivalent to the existence of a finite nonnegative bound. For measurable time slices and $T\ge0$, it implies finite kinetic energy at every time in the closed interval. Measurability is not part of this definition: without it the integral is interpreted as a lower integral, and its finiteness alone is not an assertion of $L^2$ membership. In the smooth-solution applications all time slices are measurable. The condition contains no smoothness or equation, no comparison with the initial energy, and no assertion that a single bound works as $T$ varies. The fields have values at all real times, with no restriction outside the given interval; for $T<0$ the interval is empty.
notes.Breakdown.ExtendedCertificateData: For a natural number $n$, the data contain arbitrary real functions and fields: a symmetry set $\Gamma$; the period $S(\alpha)$; the approximate profile, a proposed weak Hessian and a field representing its pressure gradient; approximate forcing coefficients and complete-field constraint targets; $n$ forcing fields and $n$ matrix constraint fields; a reference profile; a spatial weight with proposed lower and upper bounds; the finite pairing fields with weights; and all scalar bounds in the linear, nonlinear and residual estimates. They also contain an invertible-matrix candidate $V$, nonzero-scale candidates $d_j$, radii and selected coordinates for $\mathcal K$, adjoint fields, the matrix $Y$, and the adjoint and complementary-coordinate bounds. Parameters, times and space points range over all of $\mathbb R^n$, $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb R^3$. The declaration provides the objects and imposes no equations, signs, regularity, invertibility or inequalities. Those are separate certificate hypotheses. In particular these data are not intrinsically a finite machine-readable encoding: a restriction to prescribed polynomial and harmonic forms is imposed only in the later cell-data construction.

The formal functions are total in time, while the solution conditions concern $t\ge0$. No finite singular time, asymptotic rate, or same-profile statement is included.

The formal operation recovers $c(n)$ by dividing the stored sequence entry $a(n)$ by $\sqrt{1+4\pi^2|n|^2}$. The denominator is at least one, including at $n=0$; division by zero is therefore irrelevant. Thus a raw entry of the formal vector is a weighted coefficient, whereas the paper's $\hat u(n)$ is the unweighted coefficient. There is no assumption that this coefficient vanishes at zero and no spatial period parameter.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.cutoffDivergenceFree: Assume the radial-potential assertion that every smooth solenoidal $g$ has a smooth potential $A_{x_0,g}$ with $\operatorname{curl}A_{x_0,g}=g$. Here $A_{x_0,g}(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(x_0+\sigma(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,d\sigma$. In §5 take $x_0=0$, $g=u^*(t)$ and $\chi(x)=\eta(x/r)$ with $r>0$. This theorem assumes no support or size conditions on $\chi$ and therefore gives no support radius, no equality on an inner ball, and no norm bound. Its radial-potential premise is proved in the preceding curl theorem.

Derivatives and the integral are total operations: a derivative is zero where the required derivative does not exist, and a nonintegrable integral is zero. notes.Breakdown.Periodic.freeHeatComparison:
This theorem assumes the following analytic representation facts. On the unit torus, every $C^1$ periodic vector field satisfies $\widehat{\partial_jf}(k)=2\pi i k_j\widehat f(k)$. A smooth compactly supported solenoidal field transplanted at $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$ is smooth, unit-periodic, solenoidal, and agrees with its unwrapped dilation on the ball of radius $1/4$ about $(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. The whole-space heat operators form a strongly continuous self-adjoint contraction semigroup for nonnegative time and act by the multiplier $e^{-4\pi^2\max(t,0)|\xi|^2}$ on their Fourier representatives.

The proof also assumes: uniformly bounded measurable matrix multipliers after any invertible real linear frequency change have their stated almost-everywhere $L^2$ action; the direct and inverse $L^2$ Fourier transforms agree with the corresponding integrals on $L^1\cap L^2$; real $L^2$ fields have conjugate-symmetric Fourier transforms; and, when $h(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|g(\xi)$ almost everywhere for solenoidal representatives, the velocity reconstructed from $h$ equals the real inverse Fourier transform of $g$. The main construction supplies these analytic facts before using this theorem.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

For every smooth compactly supported solenoidal field $\varphi$, and every $b,\varepsilon,\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of $\mu_0>0$ such that, for $0<\mu<\mu_0$ and $0\le\tau\le\varepsilon^{-1}$, the local-data norm of the difference between the restrictions of $e^{\tau\Delta}\varphi$ and $\mu^{1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\varphi_\mu$ is at most $\delta$. This is uniform convergence on a bounded time interval, including time zero. The threshold can depend on $\varphi$ and no bound proportional to $\|\varphi\|_1$ is asserted. Formula (6.3) instead gives a uniform explicit $L^{-5/2}$ estimate for all $t>0$.
notes.Breakdown.Periodic.freqTrCoef: For a vector field $f:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $n\in\mathbb Z^3$, the formal coefficient is $\int_{[0,1]^3}e^{-2\pi i n\cdot x}f(x)\,dx\in\mathbb C^3$, with the real components of $f$ viewed as complex numbers. On integrable period-one fields this is the paper's Fourier coefficient at $L=1$. The inverse series uses $e^{2\pi i n\cdot x}$. The definition itself imposes neither periodicity nor integrability; an integral without Bochner integrability is assigned zero. At general period $L>0$, the paper's frequency is $k=n/L$ and its coefficient includes $L^{-3}$. That general-period coefficient can be expressed using $f(L\,\cdot)$, but the formal definition has no variable $L$.

This theorem assumes five representation identities. First, for every invertible real linear change of frequency variables $A$ and every strongly measurable uniformly bounded matrix multiplier $M(\xi)$, the selected $L^2$ operator agrees almost everywhere with $f\mapsto[\xi\mapsto M(\xi)f(A\xi)]$. Second, the $L^2$ Fourier transform of an $L^1\cap L^2$ complex vector field agrees almost everywhere with its Fourier integral. Third, the Fourier transform of a real $L^2$ vector field satisfies $\widehat f(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat f(\xi)}$. Fourth, if two solenoidal Fourier representatives satisfy $h(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|g(\xi)$ almost everywhere, the velocity reconstructed from $h$ is the real inverse Fourier transform of $g$. Fifth, the inverse $L^2$ Fourier transform of an $L^1\cap L^2$ field agrees almost everywhere with its inverse Fourier integral. The Fourier convention is $\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\,dx$. These are hypotheses of this particular proof theorem; the main construction supplies their proofs.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Let $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce coordinates modulo integers to the unit cell centered at $a$. Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

Given $b,b^{\prime},\varepsilon,\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of $\mu_0>0$ such that, for $0<\mu<\mu_0$, every $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$ and every $A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ supported almost everywhere in $\bar B_{b^{\prime}}$, the difference between the restricted whole-space field $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb PA$ and the restricted rescaled unit-torus field is at most $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$. The latter field is $\mu^{-1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[A((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)]$ before the periodic restriction. Compact support makes $\|A\|_{3/2}$ finite. Let $U$ be the real inverse Fourier transform of $F$, and let $P$ be the real inverse Fourier transform of $-\xi\cdot\widehat{(U\cdot\nabla)U}/(2\pi i|\xi|^2)$. The formal statement gives smoothness of both fields on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^3$, incompressibility on the closed interval, and the viscosity-one momentum equation for $0<t<T$. Division by zero assigns the pressure coefficient at $\xi=0$ the value zero; changing one frequency does not change the inverse Fourier integral. The hypotheses contain all spatial Sobolev orders and the integral equation, rather than smooth initial data alone.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.isCo:
Let $X$ be a real inner-product space and $T:X\to X$ a bounded compact real-linear operator.

The formal statement proves that $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$ is compact on the complexification, whose norm satisfies $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$. The conclusion justifies carrying the compact difference between the monodromy and the free operator into the complex setting. It is separate from the equality of their real and complex operator norms and from every assertion about the essential spectrum.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.Complexification.norm:
Let $X$ be a real inner-product space and $T:X\to X$ a bounded real-linear operator. Its complexification acts on pairs written $x+iy$ by $T_{\mathbb C}(x+iy)=Tx+iTy$, with norm $\|x+iy\|^2=\|x\|^2+\|y\|^2$.

The formal statement proves $\|T_{\mathbb C}\|\le\|T\|$. The paper says that the two norms are equal. The reverse inequality follows by restricting to the isometric copy $x\mapsto x+i0$, but is not the conclusion of this linked declaration. No compactness or spectral assumption is involved.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.exists_annulus:
Let $Y$ be a complex Banach space, let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators with $C$ compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$.

The formal statement proves that there exist $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$ such that every complex $z$ with $r_1\le|z|\le r_2$ lies in the resolvent set of $T_0+C$. Thus it gives a whole closed annulus without spectrum, which is stronger than selecting only one circle $|z|=\Theta$. In the application $\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$, any intermediate circle in this annulus can be used for the splitting. No particular numerical values for the radii are supplied.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.finite_spectrum_outsi:
Let $Y$ be a complex Banach space, $T_0,C:Y\to Y$ bounded linear operators, and suppose $C$ is compact and $\|T_0\|\le b<r$.

The formal statement proves that $\{z\in\sigma(T_0+C):|z|\ge r\}$ is finite. Since an operator norm is nonnegative, the hypotheses imply $r>0$. The spectrum is the set where $zI-(T_0+C)$ fails to have a bounded inverse. This is the finiteness conclusion used to select a circle avoiding the spectrum in Lemma 4.5. The declaration does not state equality of essential spectral radii, poles of the resolvent, or their algebraic multiplicities; those are the paper’s cited route to the same finiteness conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.norm_backProj_le:
Let $T$ be a bounded operator on a complex Banach space, and let $0<r<R$ with $\|T\|<R$ and $|z|=r$ contained in the resolvent set. Define $B_n=(2\pi i)^{-1}(\int_{|z|=R}z^{-n}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz-\int_{|z|=r}z^{-n}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz)$.

The formal statement proves that some $K>0$ satisfies $\|B_n\|\le Kr^{-n}$ for every natural $n$. A separate contour identity gives $T^nB_n=I-Q$, where $Q$ is the interior projection; this identifies the exterior inverse powers. Choosing $r>\Theta$ yields summability after multiplication by $\Theta^n$. Both contours have positive radius, so the powers $z^{-n}$ never divide by zero on them.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.norm_pow_mul_specProj:
Let $T$ be a bounded linear operator on a complex Banach space, and let $r>0$ with every point of $|z|=r$ in the resolvent set. Put $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$.

The formal statement proves the existence of $K>0$ such that $\|T^nQ\|\le Kr^n$ for every natural $n\ge0$. This is a contour-integral power estimate, stated at the contour radius. To obtain the first series of (4.11), use a radius $r<\Theta$ in the spectrum-free annulus and the equality of projections for those circles, then sum $K(r/\Theta)^n$. It gives the needed geometric bound without identifying the constant with the paper’s implicit constant.
notes.Breakdown.Spectral.specProj: For a bounded operator $T$ on a complex Banach space and real radius $r$, this defines $Q=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|z|=r}(zI-T)^{-1}\,dz$, with the circle traversed counterclockwise. If $r>0$ and the circle lies in the resolvent set, this is the spectral projection for the spectrum inside the circle. The paper denotes the projection for the exterior spectrum by $P$; with its $\Theta=r$, the corresponding operator is $P=I-Q$. The definition alone requires neither a spectral gap nor idempotence, and its total resolvent takes the value zero when an inverse does not exist. The spectral theorems impose the resolvent-set hypothesis before interpreting the integral as a projection.

Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+P)=\rho w(s)$ with $P>0$. Put $S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-P/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-P/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-P/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nP/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

This declaration specifies the assertion; it supplies no proof by itself.
notes.Breakdown.Symmetry: A symmetry is a pair $(R,\theta_0)$, where $R$ is an invertible real linear isometry of Euclidean $\mathbb R^3$ and $\theta_0\in\mathbb R$. Thus $R\in O(3)$; orientation reversal is allowed. A collection $\Gamma$ is an arbitrary set of such pairs and may be empty. Neither closure under composition nor a group structure is required. Invariance of a field under a pair is a separate condition.

notes.Breakdown.UniqueStatement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. This assertion says that two mild solutions $u,v:\mathbb R\to\mathcal X$ with $u(a)=v(a)$ coincide throughout $[a,b)$ if both are continuous and satisfy the quadratic Duhamel equation there, and throughout $[a,b]$ if both satisfy the closed-interval version. Each Duhamel integral is required to be Bochner integrable. The initial and final times are finite real numbers. Equality is asserted only on the indicated interval; arbitrary values assigned outside it are unrestricted. There is no smallness assumption on the common datum or on the length of the interval. The closed-interval conclusion is the uniqueness clause of Lemma 3.5, and the half-open conclusion is also included.
notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralInternal.conti: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Assume that $G(t)$, $t\geq0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup, and that $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear map on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. If $\tau,w,z$ are continuous maps on a subset $E$ of any topological space, with $\tau(x)>0$ for every $x\in E$, then $x\mapsto K(\tau(x))(w(x),z(x))$ is continuous on $E$. Taking $E=(0,\infty)\times\mathcal X\times\mathcal X$ gives the joint continuity used in Lemma 3.3. No assertion at $\tau=0$ is made.

Assume $\|K(\tau)\|\leq C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\leq1$ and $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ for $s\geq0$, $\tau>0$. notes.Breakdown.VarConstIntegralStatement: Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Banach space. Write $G(t)$ for a strongly continuous contraction semigroup on $t\ge0$, and let $K(\tau)$ be bounded symmetric real bilinear maps on $\mathcal X$, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of arguments. Assume $G(t)K(\tau)=K(t+\tau)$ for $t\ge0,\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)(u,v)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}\|u\|\|v\|$ for $0<\tau\le1$. In addition, when $t-a\le1$, its norm is at most $4C_K(t-a)^{1/4}MN$. Such finite $M,N$ exist by compactness of $[a,b]$. Integrability and continuity have no restriction on $b-a$. The interval of length zero is allowed, with integral zero. Values of the curves outside $[a,b]$ and the value of $K(0)$ do not affect the conclusion.
notes.Breakdown.WeakPeriodicSimilarityProfileE:
There exist $S>0$, an orthogonal map $R$, fields $W(s,y)$, $G(s,y)$ and $H(s,y)$ each admitting a measurable representative for space-time Lebesgue measure, and a finite real $C$, with the following properties. The velocity $W$ is defined on all of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$, and $W(s+S,y)=RW(s,R^{-1}y)$ at every point. For every $s$, $G(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional spatial derivative of $W(s,\cdot)$; for almost every $s$, $H(s,\cdot)$ is the distributional derivative of $G(s,\cdot)$. These distributional derivative conditions include local integrability. The velocity is divergence-free almost everywhere in space at every time. One constant bounds $\int|W(s)|^6\,dy$ and $\int\|G(s)\|^2\,dy$ for every $s$, and $\int_0^S\int\|H\|^2\,dy\,ds<\infty$. The norms of $G,H$ are operator norms; they differ by fixed dimension-dependent factors from the sums of squared coordinate derivatives used in the paper. For every smooth, compactly supported, divergence-free space-time test field $\varphi$, the integrand is integrable and
$\int_{\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3}[-W\cdot\partial_s\varphi-W\cdot\varphi-\frac12W\cdot(y\cdot\nabla)\varphi+\sum_iG(e_i)\cdot\partial_i\varphi-\sum_iW_iW\cdot\partial_i\varphi],ds\,dy=0$.
Finally $W$ is not zero almost everywhere in space-time. The expression is the pressure-free weak similarity equation: the pressure term disappears because the test fields are divergence-free. No pressure, smoothness, pointwise decay, quantitative closeness to an approximate field, or prescribed value of $R$ is part of this conclusion. Nontriviality here means nonzero on a set of positive space-time measure, rather than merely at a single point.
notes.Breakdown.WeakProfile.constOfWeakDeriv_h: Let $l<r$ and let $a,b$ be integrable real functions on $(l,r)$. Assume $\int\eta'(t)a(t)\,dt=\int\eta(t)b(t)\,dt$ for every smooth real test function supported compactly in $(l,r)$. The formal statement gives a real constant $c$ such that $a(t)=c-\int_l^tb(\tau)\,d\tau$ for almost every $t\in(l,r)$. The negative sign follows from the stated integration-by-parts convention. The conclusion provides an absolutely continuous representative through the integral; it does not assert that the original everywhere-defined $a$ is continuously differentiable, or that $b$ is continuous. The printed argument invokes stronger continuity to obtain a pointwise derivative identity. The integral in this theorem has its ordinary value because integrability is assumed.
